title: Missing data
story:
A cell is empty, and everything downstream needs something in it. So the choice is never whether to make an assumption about the absent value — the choice is which assumption, and whether you make it knowing that you did.

The conditions under which you are allowed to ignore the question were settled in 1976, in Rubin's paper in Biometrika. Two results. For sampling distribution inference, the process causing the absence can be ignored if the missing data are missing at random and the observed data are observed at random. For direct likelihood and Bayesian inference, it can be ignored if the missing data are missing at random and the parameter governing the missingness is distinct from the parameter you care about. He argues these are the weakest general conditions under which ignoring the process always yields correct inferences — which is the useful framing. Ignorability is not the normal state of affairs that you depart from in bad cases. It is a property you have to earn.

A correction to the way this is usually taught. The three-way taxonomy that gets attributed wholesale to that paper is not in it in its modern form. Rubin's own terms are missing at random and observed at random, and the combination of the two is what is now conventionally called missing completely at random. The modern labels are a later tidying, and knowing that saves you from arguing about definitions with someone who has read the source.

Here is the part that makes this hard rather than merely fiddly. The conditions are assumptions about a mechanism that lives outside the dataset, and the worst case is precisely the one the data cannot reveal. If whether a value is absent depends on the value itself — incomes missing because they are high, symptoms unrecorded because the patient was too unwell to report them — then nothing in the observed rows can tell you so, because the value that would settle the question is the one that is gone. You can test whether missingness correlates with what you did observe. You cannot test whether it correlates with what you did not.

Which is why the default remedy is the wrong one so often. Filling a column's holes with the column mean feels neutral and is not: it asserts the strongest of the conditions without checking, it puts every filled row exactly at the centre so the column's spread is understated and correlations are dragged toward zero, and it throws away the one thing you definitely knew, which is which rows were missing. That last fact is frequently more predictive than the value would have been. Keep it as its own column.

problem.name: Missingness mechanism
problem.shape: Values are absent, every downstream step needs something in the cell, and what you put there encodes an assumption about why it was absent.
tell: holes were filled before anyone asked why they were holes
the fill is a single central value applied to every missing row
the proportion missing differs noticeably between groups
nobody has checked whether missingness itself predicts the target
problem.move: Ask what produced the absence before choosing what replaces it. Record the fact of missingness as its own column first, since it is an observation. Then match the remedy to the mechanism: a simple fill only where the absence looks unrelated to anything, conditional imputation where it relates to observed columns, and an explicit model or a stated limitation where it may relate to the missing value itself. Compute any fill statistic on the training portion alone.
problem.invariant: Ignoring the missingness process is valid only under stated conditions on that process, and those conditions are the weakest under which ignoring it always gives correct inferences. Ignorability is earned by argument about the mechanism, not assumed by default.
problem.breaks: The conditions concern a mechanism outside the dataset, and the most damaging case is the one the data cannot reveal. You can test whether absence correlates with what you observed; you cannot test whether it correlates with what you did not, because the value that would settle it is the one missing.

cost.time: an indicator column and an argument about the mechanism, against a fill that takes one line and hides everything it assumed
cost.space: one boolean column per column that has holes
cost.beats: dropping incomplete rows, which is a fill by another name — it assumes the discarded rows were unrelated to everything, and quietly reshapes the population you are modelling

worked.problem: You filled the missing values with the column mean. What did you just do?
worked.reasoning:
Four things, three of them unintended.

First, you asserted the strongest assumption in the taxonomy without testing it. Replacing every hole with the same central value is only defensible if the holes are unrelated to anything — if they are related to the observed data, the fill should at least be conditional on it, and if they are related to the unobserved value itself, no fill is defensible and the missingness has to be modelled.

Second, you shrank the variance. Every imputed row now sits exactly at the mean, so the column's spread is understated by construction, and the more holes there were the more understated it is. Any variance the model reports, any confidence interval, any uncertainty estimate downstream inherits that and is too narrow. The dataset now looks more certain than the evidence supports.

Third, you dragged the correlations toward zero. The imputed rows carry no relationship to any other column — they are all the same number regardless of what else is in the row — so they dilute every association the complete rows contained. The model sees a weaker signal than the data holds.

Fourth, you discarded the most useful thing you actually knew. Whether a value was missing is itself an observation, and it is often more predictive than the value would have been — a blank income field on a credit form, a symptom left unrecorded, an unanswered survey item. Add an indicator column for the missingness before filling anything, and keep it.

What to do instead depends on which case you are in, and the point of naming the cases is that they dictate different remedies. If the absence looks unrelated to anything observed, mean or median filling is defensible and you should still keep the indicator. If it relates to observed columns, impute conditionally on them, and prefer multiple imputation if the uncertainty matters, because a single fill hides the fact that you guessed. If it relates to the unobserved value itself, no imputation rescues you: the mechanism has to be part of the model, or the limitation has to be stated plainly in the write-up.

And one mechanical thing regardless of case: whatever statistic you fill with must be computed on the training portion alone. A mean taken over the whole dataset before splitting carries information from the held-out rows into training.
worked.code:
A HOLE IS NOT A ZERO AND NOT A NEUTRAL FILL

  the question is not WHETHER to assume.
  it is WHICH assumption, and whether you know
  you made it.

THE CONDITIONS (Rubin, Biometrika, 1976)

  sampling distribution inference:
     ignorable IF missing at random
                AND observed at random

  direct likelihood / Bayesian:
     ignorable IF missing at random
                AND the missingness parameter is
                    DISTINCT from the one you want

  "the weakest general conditions under which
   ignoring the process always leads to correct
   inferences"

  -> ignorability is EARNED, not assumed.

TERMINOLOGY, CORRECTED

  the modern three-way split is not in the 1976
  paper in that form.
     Rubin's terms:  missing at random
                     observed at random
     the two together == today's "missing
                        completely at random"

THE ONE YOU CANNOT TEST

  does missingness depend on the MISSING VALUE?

     incomes absent BECAUSE they are high
     symptoms unrecorded BECAUSE too unwell

  you can test correlation with what you OBSERVED.
  you cannot test correlation with what you did not.
  the value that would settle it is the one that
  is gone.

WHAT MEAN-FILLING ACTUALLY DID

  1. asserted the strongest condition, untested
  2. shrank the variance
       every filled row sits AT the centre
       -> intervals too narrow, model overconfident
  3. dragged correlations toward zero
       filled rows relate to nothing
  4. threw away the fact of missingness
       often MORE predictive than the value

  -> add an indicator column BEFORE you fill.
  -> compute the fill on the TRAINING split only.

problem.practice: Take a dataset with holes. Before filling anything, add an indicator column for missingness and check whether it predicts your target — if it does, you have learned something the fill would have erased. Then compare the column's variance before and after a mean fill, and write down how much of the spread you removed.

beats.broke: A value is absent and every downstream operation needs something in the cell, so the choice is not whether to assume something about it but which assumption to make, and whether the assumption is made knowingly.
beats.fix: Classify the mechanism before choosing the remedy. The conditions set out in 1976 tell you when the process can be ignored — and they are the weakest conditions under which ignoring it always works, which makes ignorability something you earn rather than a default.
beats.cost: The classification is an assumption about a mechanism outside the data, and the case that most needs detecting is the one the data cannot reveal: if absence depends on the absent value itself, the evidence that would show it is exactly what is missing.

interview.q: You filled the missing values with the column mean. What did you just do?
interview.trap: Treating it as a neutral, harmless default because it changes no other column. It asserts the strongest condition in the taxonomy, understates the spread, weakens every correlation, and deletes the fact of missingness — which is often the most predictive thing in the table.
interview.answer:
Four things, and three of them were not intended.

I asserted the strongest assumption available without testing it. Filling every hole with one central value is only defensible when the absences are unrelated to anything — if they relate to the observed columns the fill should be conditional on those, and if they relate to the missing value itself no fill is defensible at all.

I shrank the variance. Every imputed row now sits exactly at the mean, so the column's spread is understated by construction, in proportion to how many holes there were. Every uncertainty estimate downstream inherits that and comes out too narrow, which means the analysis looks more certain than the evidence warrants.

I pulled the correlations toward zero. The filled rows carry the same value regardless of what else is in them, so they relate to nothing and dilute whatever association the complete rows held. The model now sees less signal than the data actually contains.

And I destroyed the one thing I definitely knew. Whether a value was missing is itself an observation, and it is frequently more predictive than the value would have been — a blank income field, an unrecorded symptom, an unanswered item. The indicator column should be created before anything is filled.

What I would do instead depends on the mechanism, which is the reason for naming the cases at all. Unrelated to anything: a simple fill, plus the indicator. Related to observed columns: impute conditionally, and use multiple imputation if the uncertainty matters, since a single fill hides that a guess occurred. Related to the unobserved value: no imputation saves it — model the mechanism or state the limitation.

Regardless of case, the fill statistic is computed on the training portion only. A mean taken across everything before splitting moves information from the held-out rows into training.

blueprint:
THREE MECHANISMS, THREE REMEDIES

   unrelated to anything
      -> a simple fill is defensible
         (still keep the indicator)

   related to what you DID observe
      -> impute CONDITIONALLY on it
         multiple imputation if uncertainty matters

   related to the value ITSELF
      -> no fill rescues you.
         model the mechanism, or state the
         limitation in the write-up.

WHY THE THIRD IS THE HARD ONE

   it is undetectable from inside the data.
   the value that would settle the question
   is the missing one.

WHAT A MEAN FILL COSTS

   variance      shrinks    (every fill at centre)
   correlations  -> 0       (fills relate to nothing)
   uncertainty   understated
   missingness   DESTROYED  (and it was evidence)

THE TWO HABITS

   1. add a was-missing indicator BEFORE filling.
      the fact of absence is an observation.

   2. compute any fill statistic on the TRAINING
      split alone. a mean over everything carries
      held-out rows into training.

THE FRAME TO KEEP

   ignorability is a property you EARN
   by argument about the mechanism,
   not a default you depart from.
takeaway: Ignoring why a value is absent is valid only under conditions you have to argue for, and the damaging case — absence that depends on the absent value — is undetectable from inside the data, which is why the fact of missingness should become a column before anything gets filled.
